title: Pressure-cooker dried beans
subtitle: Perfectly cooked haricot beans without overnight soaking
excerpt: Dried haricot beans cooked under pressure in about 35 minutes from dry. No soaking needed. The result is tender, flavourful beans ready for cassoulet, soups, or simply dressed with olive oil.
sourceNotes: Cooking dried legumes under pressure is documented across French, Italian, and American pressure-cooking literature. The no-soak method produces tender, intact beans without the overnight wait; cooking times vary by bean variety.

recipe.freezeNotes: Cool cooked beans and freeze in portions with some cooking liquid for up to 6 months.
recipe.batchNotes: Cook a large batch and refrigerate or freeze in tinned-tomato-tin-sized portions to use in recipes calling for a 400 g tin.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Cooked beans keep refrigerated in their liquid for up to 5 days.

content.text: Dried haricot beans have much better flavour than tinned. The pressure cooker makes them fast enough to cook without planning ahead. About 35 minutes at high pressure produces tender, creamy beans. No soaking needed.

Haricot beans are the classic choice: small, creamy-white, with a mild flavour that suits cassoulet, soups, and baked beans alike. The cooking liquid is starchy and flavourful, use it in the same dish or add it to soups.
Do not add salt or acid (tomatoes, lemon juice, vinegar) until after the beans are cooked. Salt and acid toughen the skins and slow down the cooking, add them only at the finish.

Put the rinsed haricot beans into the pressure cooker. Add cold water to cover by at least 5 cm, the beans will expand. Add the garlic, bay leaf, and olive oil. Do not add salt. Seal the lid and bring to high pressure. Cook at high pressure for 35 minutes. Allow a natural pressure release for at least 15 minutes, do not quick-release, as this can toughen the skins.

Open the lid and test the beans, they should be tender all the way through with no chalky centre. If undercooked, return to high pressure for a further 10 minutes. Once cooked, season with salt. Remove the bay leaf. Use immediately or cool in the cooking liquid before refrigerating or freezing.

rows.symptom: The beans are still firm in the centre
rows.cause: Old dried beans take longer to cook than fresh stock. Beans more than a year old can be significantly slower.
rows.fix: Return to high pressure for 15 to 20 minutes more. For next time, buy beans from a shop with high turnover.

rows.symptom: The beans have burst and are falling apart
rows.cause: The pressure cooker exceeded the cooking time, or a quick release was used.
rows.fix: The beans are still edible and usable in soups or purées. For a dish where whole beans are needed, reduce cooking time by 5 minutes and always use natural pressure release.

rows.symptom: The beans are tough despite long cooking
rows.cause: Salt or acid was added before cooking, this hardens the skins.
rows.fix: Never add salt, tomatoes, lemon juice, or vinegar to dried beans before they are fully cooked. Season only when the beans are tender.

content.text: Cooking beans from dried rather than tinned is worth the extra step: the flavour is cleaner, the texture is better, and a 250 g bag of dried haricot costs a fraction of the equivalent in tins. The pressure cooker removes the only real barrier, the time. Keep a cooked batch in the fridge and use it across the week: in a simple soup, dressed with olive oil and herbs as a side, or baked with tomatoes and smoked bacon for the classic British version.
